Abstract Accurate mapping of shallow-water environments using unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery is challenged by water-induced distortions, including refraction, caustics, and wavelength-dependent attenuation. The scarcity of paired distorted and reference imagery further limits the development of supervised restoration methods. To address this challenge, we introduce KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset combining 1,280 reference patches derived from 32 high-resolution UAV images with 12,800 degraded observations generated through Blender-based water-surface rendering and empirical color and blur augmentations. We further propose KAUSTics-Net, a pixel-space conditional diffusion framework integrating a multi-scale conditional encoder, feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), cross-attention, and a composite reconstruction objective to restore shallow-water imagery. We evaluated the framework against eight image-restoration methods, complemented by architectural ablations and cross-dataset experiments. On KAUSTics, KAUSTics-Net achieved a mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 31.715 ± 0.439 31.715\pm 0.439 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.849 ± 0.002 0.849\pm 0.002 , and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) of 0.145 ± 0.007 0.145\pm 0.007 across three training seeds. On the independent Sea-Undistort dataset, sampler-aware fine-tuning improved restoration fidelity, reaching 19.469 ± 0.332 19.469\pm 0.332 dB PSNR and 0.554 ± 0.005 0.554\pm 0.005 SSIM under combined water-surface distortions, although perceptual trade-offs remained. Additional experiments on real UAV imagery examined feature preservation and segmentation behavior. These findings demonstrate the potential of semi-synthetic training and conditional diffusion for shallow-water image restoration while highlighting the importance of evaluating both reconstruction fidelity and downstream remote-sensing utility. Index Terms: Caustics, Conditional Diffusion, Image Restoration, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Remote Sensing, Shallow Water. I Introduction Coastal regions support critical ecosystems, including coral reefs, seagrass meadows, mangroves, and tidal flats, while also hosting substantial populations and infrastructure. Their monitoring is essential for ecosystem assessment, coastal management, restoration, and climate adaptation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Although in situ surveys provide detailed observations, they are spatially limited, logistically demanding, and often unable to capture rapid changes in dynamic coastal environments [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Satellite and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) remote sensing provide broader and more frequent coverage, enabling shallow-water mapping at scales impractical for field surveys alone [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Extracting reliable information from optical imagery over shallow coastal waters nevertheless remains challenging. Surface waves focus and defocus sunlight, producing dynamic, high-frequency caustic patterns unrelated to actual seabed variability [ 11 , 12 ] . Specular reflection at the air–water interface generates sun glint that can saturate parts of the image and obscure the underlying scene [ 13 , 14 ] . Refraction displaces apparent object locations and distorts submerged shapes, while wavelength-dependent absorption and scattering alter the signal returning from the seafloor. Together, these effects degrade contrast and color, distort geometry, and complicate applications such as benthic habitat mapping [ 15 ] , bathymetry [ 16 ] , and photogrammetry [ 17 ] . Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate water-induced distortions. Physics-based methods invert simplified radiative-transfer models but often require estimates of water depth, optical properties, and atmospheric conditions [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . Image-processing approaches apply deglinting, dehazing, contrast enhancement, or multi-view corrections [ 21 , 16 , 12 ] . More recently, deep learning has enabled data-driven mappings between distorted and reference imagery. GAN-based methods have been applied to underwater enhancement and coastal water removal [ 22 , 13 , 23 ] , while diffusion-based image-to-image models have demonstrated capabilities for removing complex degradations while preserving scene structure [ 24 , 25 ] . However, learning-based restoration of shallow-water UAV imagery is constrained by the scarcity of large, high-resolution paired datasets containing observations of the same scene with and without water-surface distortions [ 23 , 26 ] . Repeated acquisitions under different sea states and illumination rarely provide aligned pairs and make it difficult to separate water-surface effects from genuine scene changes [ 10 ] . Purely synthetic data, in contrast, may not capture the spatial complexity and variability of real coastal environments. This motivates semi-synthetic approaches that combine real UAV imagery with physically based simulations of water-induced distortions. To address this gap, we introduce KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset for high-resolution UAV water-distortion removal, together with KAUSTics-Net, a conditional diffusion-based restoration framework. We evaluated the proposed approach on KAUSTics and the independent Sea-Undistort benchmark [ 26 ] , complemented by an exploratory assessment on real UAV imagery. In summary, this work makes the following contributions: • We introduce KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset comprising 1,280 high-resolution UAV reference patches and 12,800 degraded observations generated through physically based water-surface rendering and empirical color and blur augmentations. • We propose KAUSTics-Net, a pixel-space conditional diffusion framework combining multi-scale conditioning, FiLM-modulated residual blocks, cross-attention, and a composite restoration objective for through-water UAV imagery. • We evaluate KAUSTics-Net against eight restoration methods using source-image-disjoint partitions, architectural ablations, cross-dataset experiments, and real-UAV assessments of downstream image-processing utility. II Related Work Image restoration has been extensively studied across computer vision and remote sensing, including dehazing, deblurring, deraining, and underwater image enhancement. However, methods explicitly targeting water-surface distortions such as caustics, sun glint, and refraction in high-resolution UAV imagery remain comparatively limited. In practice, many approaches applied to this problem were originally developed for generic image restoration or underwater cameras rather than through-water aerial observations [ 27 , 23 , 28 ] . Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into statistical and physics-based corrections, generative adversarial networks (GANs), and diffusion-based restoration models. II-A Statistical and Physics-Based Approaches In UAV-based shallow-water imaging, refraction at the air–water interface displaces apparent object locations and distorts submerged shapes, while wave-induced caustics and sun glint introduce strong spatially varying radiometric artifacts [ 29 , 12 ] . Early correction methods primarily focused on geometric effects by applying empirical refraction factors derived from Snell’s law. Partama et al. proposed a correction of apparent depths from UAV structure-from-motion reconstructions, while related studies incorporated refraction correction into shallow-water bathymetric inversion schemes [ 30 , 31 ] . Reviews of UAV-based shallow-water bathymetry have highlighted the effectiveness of these approaches, but also their dependence on acquisition geometry, water depth, seabed properties, and assumptions regarding the water surface [ 32 , 33 ] . A complementary family of methods exploits temporal redundancy in high-frame-rate imagery. Fluid lensing uses repeated observations of the same scene to model the dynamic water surface as a time-varying optical lens and reconstruct refraction-corrected, caustic-reduced imagery [ 34 , 35 ] . More recently, Scilla et al. showed that frame-wise temporal aggregation combined with color-transfer correction can reduce caustics, refraction-induced shape variations, and sun glint in UAV video while improving the consistency of submerged features [ 12 ] . Although effective, these approaches generally rely on explicit physical assumptions, hand-crafted corrections, or repeated observations of the same scene. They therefore do not directly learn a single-image mapping from a distorted observation to a clean seabed representation, motivating the use of data-driven generative models. II-B Generative Adversarial Networks Generative adversarial networks learn image distributions through competition between a generator and discriminator [ 36 ] , and have been widely adopted for image enhancement and restoration. In image-to-image translation, CycleGAN introduced cycle consistency for learning mappings between unpaired image domains [ 37 ] , a particularly useful property when paired distorted and clean observations are difficult to acquire. Underwater enhancement models such as UGAN, FUnIE-GAN, MLFcGAN, and UWGAN use adversarial learning to improve color balance, contrast, local structure, and, in some cases, downstream robotic perception [ 27 , 38 , 39 , 40 ] . These approaches have demonstrated substantial improvements for imagery acquired by underwater cameras. However, their target domain differs from through-water UAV imagery, where wave-induced refraction, dynamic caustics, and sun glint introduce stronger spatially varying geometric and radiometric distortions. Only a limited number of GAN-based methods have directly addressed aerial water removal. DeWaterGAN is a physics-guided unsupervised framework for UAV coastal imagery that combines a CycleGAN backbone with a light-transport-inspired attention mechanism [ 23 ] . The model can reduce water interference while preserving color and texture, but it primarily targets appearance restoration and does not rely on pixel-aligned distorted/undistorted training pairs. Overall, GAN-based methods demonstrate the potential of learned restoration, but their application to through-water UAV imagery remains challenging, as these images belong to substantially different domains, containing stronger refraction induced distortions, and complex caustic patterns that are not fully captured in classical underwater datasets. II-C Diffusion and Advanced Restoration Models Denoising diffusion probabilistic models progressively corrupt training data with Gaussian noise and learn the reverse denoising process [ 41 ] . Latent diffusion models, including Stable Diffusion, further reduce computational cost by performing this process in a compressed representation space [ 42 ] . Conditional diffusion models extend this framework to image-to-image restoration by incorporating degraded observations into the denoising process. For instance, Palette introduced a general conditional diffusion framework for image-to-image translation [ 43 ] . Several diffusion-based approaches have been developed for underwater image enhancement. UW-DDPM introduced a dual-U-Net formulation with distribution-fusion sampling [ 44 ] , while DiffWater incorporated degraded-image and color-compensated guidance to improve underwater image restoration [ 28 ] . Related studies have investigated accelerated sampling strategies and alternative conditioning mechanisms [ 45 , 46 ] . Beyond underwater imagery, NDR-Restore learns degradation representations to address multiple corruption types [ 47 ] , while ResShift formulates diffusion in the residual space between degraded and reference images to reduce the number of sampling steps [ 48 ] . Alternative deep learning architectures have also been developed for underwater image enhancement. SS-UIE combines spatial selective scanning and spectral attention to address nonuniform image degradation [ 49 ] , while U-Shape Transformer integrates multi-scale channel-wise feature fusion and spatial global modeling [ 50 ] . These methods provide complementary restoration strategies beyond conventional convolutional and diffusion-based frameworks. More recently, the Sea-Undistort dataset introduced a paired synthetic benchmark for through-water airborne imagery and evaluated restoration models under sun glint, scattering, and wave-induced distortions [ 26 ] . These results demonstrate the potential of learning-based restoration for aerial through-water observations. However, most existing restoration methods were developed for underwater-camera imagery or general image degradation rather than through-water UAV observations. Moreover, the availability of large paired datasets preserving the texture and spatial complexity of real coastal UAV imagery remains limited. The present work addresses this gap by introducing KAUSTics, a semi-synthetic dataset combining real high-resolution UAV imagery with rendered water-surface distortions and empirical appearance augmentations, together with KAUSTics-Net, a conditional diffusion framework tailored to this setting. This combination enables supervised restoration toward calm-water reference imagery and controlled evaluation under multiple caustic patterns, blur levels, and color transformations. III Methodology III-A KAUSTics Dataset The KAUSTics dataset builds on UAV surveys conducted in June 2024 between 8 and 9 AM at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), approximately 80 km north of Jeddah on the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia (22.34 ∘ N, 39.09 ∘ E). The surveys were originally collected for coastal monitoring applications, including habitat mapping. For this study, we selected 32 images acquired over a shallow-water lagoon (depth < 3 <3 m; Fig. 1 ) under clear-sky and low-wind conditions to minimize visible water-surface distortions. The images were acquired using a DJI Matrice 300 RTK flying at 35 m altitude and equipped with a Zenmuse P1 45-MP full-frame camera with a 35 mm lens. Each frame had a resolution of 8192 × 5460 8192\times 5460 pixels and a ground sampling distance of approximately 0.4 ​ c ​ m / p ​ i ​ x ​ e ​ l 0.4~cm/pixel . The surveyed area included sandy, rocky, seagrass, and macroalgal substrates. The selected images represent different seabed textures and visual characteristics observed in the lagoon and serve as calm-water reference targets. Their geometric and radiometric accuracy has not been independently established. Fig. 1: Area of interest for the KAUSTics dataset. The background shows a Sentinel-2 RGB composite of the coastal waters near Thuwal, Saudi Arabia, in the central Red Sea. The orange lines indicate the approximate area of interest of the UAV surveys used to acquire the calm-water reference imagery over shallow reef flats and sandy substrates. Synthetic surface distortions were generated using Blender [ 51 ] by mapping the UAV-derived reference imagery onto the bottom plane of a virtual shallow-water scene and rendering it through a simulated water surface. The rendering process introduced wave-induced illumination focusing (caustics) and refractive displacement. Sun glint was not independently parameterized or controlled in the KAUSTics rendering process. The virtual camera was configured to provide a reproducible nadir-viewing geometry at an altitude of 10 m, with a sensor size of 13.2 × 8.8 13.2\times 8.8 mm, a focal length of 6.201 mm, and a rendering resolution of 1000 × 1000 1000\times 1000 pixels. The rendering setup is illustrated in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2: Rendering setup used to generate the synthetic component of KAUSTics. (a) Blender scene showing the UAV-derived seafloor texture mapped onto the bottom plane and viewed by a nadir-looking camera. (b) Mesh of the simulated water surface generated using the Ocean Modifier, with a central zoom showing its spatial sampling density. Water-surface geometry was simulated using Blender’s Ocean Modifier with the Shallow Water spectrum, a depth parameter of 0.4 m, Spatial Size of 49 m, wave-amplitude Scale of 0.025, and wind velocity of 5 m s -1 . The geometry Size parameter was set to 0.190, with a water-object scale of approximately 1.665. Two distinct caustic patterns were generated by varying the surface alignment parameters: Shape 1 used an alignment of 0, producing predominantly cell-like caustics, whereas Shape 2 used an alignment of 0.1, a direction of 90°, and damping of 0.5, producing more parallel structures (Fig. 3 ). Surface realizations were varied through the Ocean Modifier’s random seed. All scenes were rendered using Blender Cycles with OptiX acceleration on an NVIDIA A100 GPU (80 GB). These parameters define the synthetic scene configuration and do not represent measured hydrodynamic or optical properties of the lagoon. Fig. 3: Overview of the KAUSTics semi-synthetic dataset. UAV imagery is divided into 1000 × 1000 1000\times 1000 pixel reference patches and rendered in Blender to generate two caustic patterns. Gaussian blur and three empirical color-transfer configurations (Color 1–3) expand the dataset to ten degraded observations per reference patch. The resulting dataset follows the hierarchical organization illustrated in Fig. 3 . Starting from the rendered caustic patterns, Gaussian-blurred variants were generated to approximate reduced visibility and optical defocus. Three additional color transformations (Color 1–3) were applied using statistical color transfer in CIELAB space [ 52 ] , matching channel means and standard deviations to manually selected target appearances. These transformations introduce variability in spectral appearance and serve as empirical proxies for absorption- and turbidity-like effects. They do not constitute calibrated simulations of water-column optical properties or measured depth-dependent attenuation. Each of the 32 UAV images contributed 40 reference patches of 1000 × 1000 1000\times 1000 pixels, resulting in 1,280 reference patches. Each reference was associated with ten degraded observations: two caustic patterns, two Gaussian-blurred variants, and six color-transfer variants corresponding to three color configurations applied to both caustic patterns. The complete dataset therefore comprises 12,800 distorted–reference pairs. These augmentations increase the diversity of simulated degradation appearances without increasing the number of independent source images. The source-image-disjoint training, validation, and test partitioning protocol is described in Section III-G . Although each degraded observation is associated with its corresponding reference patch, wave-induced refraction can introduce local geometric displacement, preventing exact feature-wise pixel correspondence. The calm-water references were acquired through water and may retain residual refraction and radiometric attenuation. No independent water-free seabed images, surveyed geometric references, or calibrated reflectance measurements are available. Consequently, KAUSTics supports supervised restoration toward a low-distortion, calm-water reference appearance. Additional dataset visualizations and rendering specifications are provided in the supplementary material. III-B Sea-Undistort Dataset To assess the generalization of KAUSTics-Net beyond the KAUSTics dataset, we also evaluated it on Sea-Undistort [ 26 ] , a synthetic through-water benchmark developed in Blender for airborne bathymetric mapping. The dataset comprises 1,200 scenes, originally rendered as 512 × 512 512\times 512 pixel RGB images. The simulated seabed includes randomized combinations of sandy flats, gravel, rocky substrates, and seagrass-like vegetation, providing a range of textures and reflectance characteristics. For each scene, Sea-Undistort provides an original water-free reference image and multiple distorted observations generated under different water-surface and water-column conditions, including refraction, sun glint, light absorption, and turbidity-related effects. In this study, we considered three distortion configurations: all effects , no waves , and no sunglint . The all-effects configuration combines surface-wave and water-column distortions, while the other two configurations exclude the corresponding surface effect. All three share the same water-free reference image, enabling consistent evaluation across distortion conditions. Some observations exhibit strong glint and wave-induced distortions that partially or completely obscure the seabed, increasing the difficulty of restoration. III-C KAUSTics-Net Architecture KAUSTics-Net is a pixel-space conditional diffusion framework designed to restore shallow-water UAV imagery affected by spatially varying water-induced distortions. The architecture consists of a U-Net denoiser, a multi-scale conditional encoder, feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) residual blocks, and a cross-attention bottleneck (Fig. 5 ). The model operates directly on RGB images without a latent autoencoder or pretrained diffusion components and predicts diffusion velocity conditioned on the distorted observation. Let 𝐱 0 ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 \mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} denote the reference image and 𝐱 cond ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{cond}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} its corresponding distorted observation. During training, a noisy sample 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} is generated from 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} at diffusion timestep t t , as described in Section III-D . The U-Net receives the channel-wise concatenation of 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} and 𝐱 cond \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{cond}} , while a separate five-stage conditional encoder extracts multi-scale features from the distorted observation. The encoder uses 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolutions, group normalization, SiLU activations, and bilinear downsampling, with channel dimensions of 16, 32, 64, 128, and 256. The extracted features condition the U-Net residual blocks through FiLM [ 53 ] . A 256-dimensional sinusoidal timestep embedding and globally pooled conditional features are projected into channel-wise scale and shift parameters, allowing the residual blocks to incorporate both the diffusion timestep and image-dependent information. At the 16 × 16 16\times 16 bottleneck, a single-head cross-attention mechanism with 256-dimensional features further integrates the conditioning information. U-Net features serve as queries, while projected conditional features provide keys and values. The decoder combines these representations with skip connections to predict the diffusion velocity 𝐯 θ ​ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 cond , t ) \mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{cond}},t) . This conditioning strategy is motivated by the combination of localized caustics and refractive distortions with broader radiometric changes in through-water imagery. Multi-scale features provide image-dependent information throughout denoising, while the bottleneck attention mechanism integrates spatial information from the distorted observation. The individual architectural components follow established diffusion and conditioning techniques; their contribution within KAUSTics-Net is examined through the ablation experiments. III-F Benchmark Models and Evaluation Metrics We benchmarked KAUSTics-Net against eight image-restoration methods spanning GAN-based architectures, underwater image enhancement, and diffusion-based restoration. The GAN-based baselines include CycleGAN [ 37 ] , UGAN [ 27 ] , FUnIE-GAN [ 38 ] , and DeWaterGAN [ 23 ] . The diffusion-based methods include DiffWater [ 28 ] and ResShift [ 48 ] . We additionally evaluated SS-UIE [ 49 ] and U-Shape Transformer [ 50 ] , which incorporate spatial–spectral modeling and transformer-based feature extraction, respectively. These methods provide complementary architectural comparisons for restoring imagery affected by spatially varying distortions. All eight baselines were trained and evaluated using the revised experimental protocol described in the following subsection. Restoration fidelity was assessed using mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (mPSNR), mean structural similarity index (mSSIM), mean root mean squared error (mRMSE), and mean squared error (mMSE). We additionally included learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) [ 56 ] and CIEDE2000 ( Δ ​ E 00 \Delta E_{00} ) [ 57 ] to quantify perceptual feature differences and color discrepancies relative to the reference images. Higher values indicate better performance for mPSNR and mSSIM, while lower values are preferred for the remaining metrics. LPIPS was computed using an AlexNet backbone on 8-bit RGB outputs, and CIEDE2000 was evaluated in D65/2-degree CIELAB space. No-reference image quality was evaluated using the Natural Image Quality Evaluator (NIQE) [ 58 ] , Blind/Referenceless Image Spatial Quality Evaluator (BRISQUE) [ 59 ] , Perception-based Image Quality Evaluator (PIQE) [ 60 ] , and Integrated Local NIQE (ILNIQE) [ 61 ] . These metrics assess deviations from statistical properties associated with natural images, with lower values indicating better predicted quality. Three learning-based perceptual metrics were also included: Learned Image Quality Evaluator (LIQE) [ 62 ] , CLIP-based Image Quality assessment (CLIPIQ) [ 63 ] , and Multi-scale Image Quality (MUSIQ) [ 64 ] . For MUSIQ, we report the AVA-trained variant (MUSIQ_AVA), with higher scores indicating better predicted perceptual quality. Sharpness and Shannon entropy were further computed as complementary indicators of image detail and intensity variability. Sharpness was defined as the variance of the discrete Laplacian, while entropy was calculated from the 256-bin luminance histogram. These metrics characterize changes in image structure and tonal distribution but do not independently establish restoration accuracy, as noise and artifacts can also increase their values. Finally, to investigate the potential utility of restoration for downstream UAV image analysis, we evaluated real-world examples using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [ 65 ] and scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) [ 66 ] , following the computer-vision assessment approach previously applied to shallow-water UAV imagery [ 12 ] . SAM was used to examine automatically generated image regions, while SIFT quantified local keypoint detection and descriptor correspondence. The real-UAV comparison used a temporal computer-vision reference from our previous work, which provides a low-distortion comparison image without constituting independently validated water-free ground truth. These analyses complement the image quality metrics by examining the preservation of local features and segmentation behavior. III-G Experimental Setup The stored KAUSTics images were converted to RGB and normalized to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] for training. All methods used the same 256 × 256 256\times 256 image resolution, obtained by bicubic downsampling of the original 1000 × 1000 1000\times 1000 patches without additional spatial cropping. To prevent leakage between augmented observations of the same source image, the dataset was partitioned at the UAV-image level. Using a fixed random seed of 42, the 32 source images were divided into 26 training, three validation, and three test images. Every reference patch and its ten degraded variants inherited the partition of the corresponding source image. Table II summarizes the resulting dataset composition. The partitioning protocol ensures independence of source-image identifiers across training, validation, and testing. For KAUSTics-Net, each training epoch contained 2,080 patch–shape combinations, with additional degradation variants sampled with probability 0.6.
